4	This work presents a systematic evaluation of symbolic constraint aggregation for LLM majority voting across five models, three reasoning domains, and more than 1,300 instances. \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Neuro-symbolic methods that augment large language model (LLM) reasoning with formal solvers have demonstrated gains on logical reasoning benchmarks. Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} delegate formalization to external provers. More recent systems route problems to specialized solver paradigms \citep{xu2026dylos}, apply logic-complete decomposition \citep{li2025aristotle}, train dedicated first-order logic (FOL) verifiers on supervised data \citep{wang2025fover}, or employ multi-perspective grounding \citep{luo2025logicagent}. These systems report positive results on formal reasoning benchmarks, but a critical commonality unites them: each introduces capabilities beyond the reasoning model itself, whether trained verifiers, multi-paradigm solver selection, or external knowledge bases. The external machinery is effective but imposes practical costs in training data, integration complexity, and domain-specific engineering that limits portability.

These results raise a direct question: can the reasoning model itself extract useful formal constraints from its own traces? Same-model self-extraction would require no training data, no external prover, and no second model. Practitioners could augment any LLM with symbolic verification by adding a single extraction prompt and a satisfiability solver, with no domain-specific infrastructure. If successful, this approach would provide a lightweight, portable alternative to the external machinery that current systems require. Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extraction produces constraints useful for answer aggregation, or characterized the conditions under which it succeeds or fails. This gap is consequential: the practical promise of neuro-symbolic reasoning hinges on whether the reasoning model alone can supply formal structure of sufficient quality, or whether external grounding is fundamentally required.

Self-Consistency (SC) selects the most frequent answer across multiple chain-of-thought samples \citep{wang2023sc} and remains competitive across mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning \citep{chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc}. SC treats traces as black boxes, discarding all intermediate reasoning. Each trace, however, contains intermediate steps, logical dependencies, and structural relationships that could in principle ground aggregation in formal logic, adding discriminative power beyond vote counting. This would also address SC's known scaling plateau, where additional traces yield diminishing returns \citep{loo2025reevaluating}.

We evaluate this possibility through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), a pipeline that extracts FOL constraints from $K$ reasoning traces produced by a single LLM, deduplicates by syntactic equivalence, and solves a weighted partial MAX-SAT problem via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3}. The answer best supported by the largest satisfiable constraint subset is selected (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}). We test five model families spanning 7B to 32B parameters (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, QwQ-32B), including instruction-tuned models, a reasoning-specialized model, and a distilled reasoning model, across three reasoning domains: formal logic (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}), commonsense (StrategyQA \citep{geva2021strategyqa}), and science (ARC-Challenge \citep{clark2018arc}), with supplementary probes on GSM8K \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} and AIME 2024, totaling more than 1,300 instances. An oracle control on FOLIO ($n=204$) replaces self-extracted constraints with gold FOL annotations verified by Z3, isolating extraction quality from aggregation effectiveness following established methodology \citep{press2023compositionality}.

Across all conditions, SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over SC, with accuracy gaps between $-3.3$ and $+3.3$\,pp. The oracle experiment yields a fundamentally different result: $+8.82$\,pp over SC (McNemar $p = 6.15 \times 10^{-5}$), confirming that the MAX-SAT mechanism is sound when given discriminative constraints. The bottleneck is extraction quality. Because the same model generates both answers and constraints, the extracted constraints are semantically coupled to their source answers and carry no independent signal. We term this the \emph{capability trap}: the model cannot formalize corrections to its own reasoning errors because extraction inherits the same biases that produced those errors. A constraint ablation confirms the diagnosis: MAX-SAT and count-only aggregation agree on 803 of 804 predictions (\S\ref{sec:ablation}). Manual analysis shows only 11.5\% of unique constraints evaluate differently across candidates; the remainder encode shared domain facts that contribute identical scores to every answer. Constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total SICA pipeline time, roughly doubling wall-clock cost for zero expected accuracy gain.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item We evaluate SICA across five model families and three reasoning domains ($N > 1{,}300$), finding no improvement over majority voting in any condition.
\item We design an oracle control achieving $+8.82$\,pp over SC ($p < 0.001$), causally localizing the failure to extraction quality rather than the aggregation mechanism.
\item We identify the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ as a zero-cost diagnostic: low $C_0$ rules out any possible SICA gain before constraint extraction begins.
\item We show through constraint ablation that MAX-SAT, count-only, and random-weight aggregation produce nearly identical predictions (803/804 agreement), confirming that self-extracted constraints carry no discriminative signal beyond vote counts (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation across five model families (7B to 32B parameters) and three reasoning domains with more than 1,300 total instances. Self-extracted SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over Self-Consistency in any tested condition, with accuracy gaps ranging from $-3.3$ to $+3.3$\,pp. The oracle experiment, which replaces self-extraction with gold FOL annotations verified by Z3, achieves $+8.82$ percentage points over SC ($p < 0.001$). This result causally localizes the failure to extraction quality: the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound when supplied with high-quality constraints, but same-model self-extraction cannot produce them. We identify this as a \emph{capability trap}: because the reasoning model also extracts the constraints, those constraints inherit the same biases that produced potentially flawed answers and carry no independent discriminative signal. The failure is not one of aggregation design but of the circular dependency between generation and verification within a single model.

The practical consequences are substantial. Only 11.5\% of self-extracted constraints evaluate differently across candidate answers; the remainder encode shared domain facts satisfied equally by every candidate. MAX-SAT agrees with count-only aggregation on 803 of 804 predictions, which confirms that satisfiability structure adds nothing when constraints are non-discriminative. Constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total pipeline time and roughly doubles computational cost for zero expected accuracy benefit. For practitioners who evaluate constraint-based voting, the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ serves as a zero-cost diagnostic: it is computable from trace samples alone, before any investment in constraint extraction or solver invocation. Low $C_0$ rules out any possible SICA gain by construction, and high $C_0$ signals the need for a small-scale constraint quality audit before full deployment.

The $+8.82$\,pp oracle gap quantifies recoverable potential and points to three concrete paths forward. Trained FOL extractors supervised on gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns beyond same-model capabilities. Cross-model extraction, where a separate model formalizes another model's traces, breaks the self-reference loop that produces non-discriminative constraints. External provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency entirely. Each path targets the extraction bottleneck directly; the aggregation mechanism requires no modification.

\section{Prompt Templates}
\label{app:prompts}

SICA uses domain-specific prompt templates for constraint extraction: one for mathematical reasoning (MATH, GSM8K, AIME) and one for logical reasoning (ProofWriter, FOLIO). Both share the same system prompt. The LLM is called with temperature $T{=}0.1$, max tokens $1024$, and structured JSON output mode. Up to 6 traces are processed in parallel via thread pooling, with 2 retries on failure (exponential backoff, base 0.5s).

\paragraph{System Prompt.}

\begin{lstlisting}
You are a constraint extraction tool. Output ONLY
valid JSON. Do NOT solve problems, reason about
correctness, or think step-by-step. Extract
constraints from the given trace exactly as stated.
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Mathematical Constraint Extraction (EXTRACTION\_PROMPT).}

Used for MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME datasets. The placeholder \texttt{\{trace\}} is replaced with the reasoning trace at runtime.

\begin{lstlisting}
Extract mathematical constraints from this reasoning
trace as a JSON object.

Rules:
- type: "equation", "inequality", or "predicate"
- expression: human-readable, e.g. "x + y == 14"
- z3_formula: a single comparison expression in
  Python Z3 syntax
- source_step: step number where the constraint
  appears
- Use variable names from the trace

z3_formula MUST follow these rules:
- Allowed operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=, +, -, *,
  /, **, %
- Use individual named variables: a1, a2, a3...
  NOT arrays a[1] or sets A
- Expand all sums explicitly:
  "a1 + a2 + a3 == 55" NOT "sum([a1,a2,a3])"
- NO Python builtins: sum(), len(), max(), min(),
  list(), set(), range(), int()
- Each z3_formula must be exactly ONE comparison
  (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=)
- For multiple values, write separate constraints
  for each

Output ONLY the JSON below, nothing else:
{"constraints": [{"type": "equation",
  "expression": "x + y == 14",
  "z3_formula": "x + y == 14",
  "source_step": 1}],
 "answer": "final_answer",
 "variables": ["x", "y"]}

Trace:
{trace}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Logical Constraint Extraction (LOGIC\_EXTRACTION\_PROMPT).}

Used for ProofWriter and FOLIO datasets.

\begin{lstlisting}
IMPORTANT: You are an EXTRACTION tool, NOT a problem
solver.
- Do NOT re-solve or re-reason about the problem.
- Do NOT verify whether the trace's reasoning is
  correct.
- ONLY extract the logical constraints that are
  explicitly stated or used in the trace below.
- Output ONLY the JSON object, nothing else.

Extract logical constraints from this reasoning trace
about a logic problem.

The problem has facts (base assertions), rules
(grounded implications), and derived conclusions.
Convert each into a Z3 boolean formula.

Variable naming:
- Unary property: property_entity
  (e.g., kind_anne, red_charlie, round_fiona)
- Binary relation: relation_subject_object
  (e.g., eats_bear_squirrel, likes_lion_cat)
- Use lowercase with underscores only

Constraint types:
- "fact": a given assertion,
  e.g., kind_anne == True
- "rule": a grounded implication over specific
  entities, e.g., Implies(kind_anne, nice_anne)
- "derived": an inferred conclusion from facts +
  rules, e.g., nice_anne == True

Z3 operators:
- Implies(a, b) for if-then rules
- And(a, b, ...) for conjunctive conditions
- Or(a, b, ...) for disjunctive conditions
- Not(a) for negation
- == True / == False for boolean assertions

Output ONLY the JSON below, nothing else:
{"constraints": [{"type": "fact",
  "expression": "kind(anne)",
  "z3_formula": "kind_anne == True",
  "source_step": 1}],
 "answer": "True or False or Unknown",
 "variables": ["kind_anne"]}

Trace:
{trace}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Output Schema.}

Both prompts produce a JSON object with the following structure:

\begin{lstlisting}
{
  "constraints": [
    {
      "type": "<equation|inequality|predicate>
               or <fact|rule|derived>",
      "expression": "<human-readable description>",
      "z3_formula": "<Z3-compatible expression>",
      "source_step": <integer>
    }
  ],
  "answer": "<final answer string>",
  "variables": ["<var1>", "<var2>", "..."]
}
\end{lstlisting}

The pipeline additionally injects an \texttt{answer\_assertion} constraint per trace (not produced by the LLM):

\begin{lstlisting}
{"type": "answer_assertion",
 "expression": "answer is <ans>",
 "z3_formula": "__sica_answer_<ans> == True",
 "source_step": -1}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Prompt Selection Logic.}

Domain assignment is determined by dataset: FOLIO and ProofWriter use \textsc{Logic\_Extraction\_Prompt}; MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME use \textsc{Extraction\_Prompt}.


\section{Capability Trap Diagnostics}
\label{app:diagnostics}

Table~\ref{tab:capability_trap} reports per-condition diagnostic metrics referenced in \S\ref{sec:diagnostics}.

\begin{table}[h]

\label{tab:capability_trap}
\end{table}


\section{Statistical Power Analysis}
\label{app:power}

We compute the minimum detectable effect (MDE) for each condition at $\alpha = 0.05$ and 80\% power using exact binomial power calculations over McNemar discordant pairs. Table~\ref{tab:power} reports the three conditions with $n \geq 200$, which constitute our confirmatory analyses. The remaining six conditions ($n \leq 60$) yield infinite MDE due to insufficient discordant pairs and serve only as regime characterization.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & $n$ & \textbf{MDE} & \textbf{Obs.\ $\Delta$} & \textbf{Obs.\ Pow.} \\
\midrule
Qwen-14B FOLIO+PW   & 804 & 1.86pp & $+$0.25pp & 5.7\%  \\
LLaMA-8B StrategyQA  & 200 & 4.64pp & $+$2.00pp & 20.6\% \\
LLaMA-8B FOLIO       & 204 & 4.84pp & $-$2.45pp & 18.6\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Power analysis for confirmatory conditions ($n \geq 200$). MDE = minimum detectable effect at 80\% power. All observed effects fall below their respective MDEs, and observed power remains below 21\% in every case.}
\label{tab:power}
\end{table}

The largest study (Qwen-14B, $n{=}804$, 30 discordant pairs) can detect effects as small as 1.86pp, yet the observed $\Delta$ of $+$0.25pp is an order of magnitude smaller. The two LLaMA-8B conditions require effects of 4.64pp and 4.84pp to reach significance; neither observed $\Delta$ approaches these thresholds. All three conditions are consistent with the null hypothesis that SICA provides no accuracy gain over self-consistency.


\section{Bootstrap Confidence Intervals}
\label{app:bootstrap}

We compute 95\% confidence intervals for $\Delta(\text{SICA} - \text{SC})$ via 10{,}000 bootstrap resamples (percentile method, seed 42). Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap} reports the results for the three confirmatory conditions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrl}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & $n$ & \textbf{Obs.\ $\Delta$} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Qwen-14B FOLIO+PW   & 804 & $+$0.25pp & [$-$1.12, $+$1.62] \\
LLaMA-8B StrategyQA  & 200 & $+$2.00pp & [$-$1.50, $+$5.50] \\
LLaMA-8B FOLIO       & 204 & $-$2.45pp & [$-$5.88, $+$0.98] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals for $\Delta(\text{SICA} - \text{SC})$ in percentage points. All intervals include zero, consistent with no reliable accuracy difference.}
\label{tab:bootstrap}
\end{table}

All three intervals contain zero. The narrowest interval (Qwen-14B, [$-$1.12, $+$1.62]) rules out practically meaningful gains ($>$2pp) even in the most favorable case. The widest interval (LLaMA-8B FOLIO, [$-$5.88, $+$0.98]) skews negative, indicating that SICA may slightly hurt accuracy in this condition. These results corroborate the McNemar tests and power analysis: no condition provides evidence that symbolic constraint aggregation improves over majority voting.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation across five model families (7B to 32B parameters) and three reasoning domains with more than 1,300 total instances. Self-extracted SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over Self-Consistency in any tested condition, with accuracy gaps ranging from $-3.3$ to $+3.3$\,pp. The oracle experiment, which replaces self-extraction with gold FOL annotations verified by Z3, achieves $+8.82$ percentage points over SC ($p < 0.001$). This result causally localizes the failure to extraction quality: the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound when supplied with high-quality constraints, but same-model self-extraction cannot produce them. We identify this as a \emph{capability trap}: because the reasoning model also extracts the constraints, those constraints inherit the same biases that produced potentially flawed answers and carry no independent discriminative signal. The failure is not one of aggregation design but of the circular dependency between generation and verification within a single model.

The practical consequences are substantial. Only 11.5\% of self-extracted constraints evaluate differently across candidate answers; the remainder encode shared domain facts satisfied equally by every candidate. MAX-SAT agrees with count-only aggregation on 803 of 804 predictions, which confirms that satisfiability structure adds nothing when constraints are non-discriminative. Constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total pipeline time and roughly doubles computational cost for zero expected accuracy benefit. For practitioners who evaluate constraint-based voting, the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ serves as a zero-cost diagnostic: it is computable from trace samples alone, before any investment in constraint extraction or solver invocation. Low $C_0$ rules out any possible SICA gain by construction, and high $C_0$ signals the need for a small-scale constraint quality audit before full deployment.

The $+8.82$\,pp oracle gap quantifies recoverable potential and points to three concrete paths forward. Trained FOL extractors supervised on gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns beyond same-model capabilities. Cross-model extraction, where a separate model formalizes another model's traces, breaks the self-reference loop that produces non-discriminative constraints. External provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency entirely. Each path targets the extraction bottleneck directly; the aggregation mechanism requires no modification.

Several limitations bound the scope of our conclusions. First, the oracle experiment is restricted to FOLIO ($n = 204$), the only benchmark in our study with gold FOL annotations; extending this analysis to other domains requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets. Second, six of our ten model-domain conditions have $n \leq 60$, providing insufficient statistical power for confirmatory claims; these conditions serve as regime characterization rather than definitive tests. Third, we do not compare against trained FOL extractors or cross-model extraction pipelines; our findings characterize the limitations of same-model self-extraction specifically. Fourth, all models tested range from 7B to 32B parameters; whether the capability trap persists at larger scales (70B+) remains an open question. Fifth, the GSM8K pilot ($n = 30$) is included to illustrate the constraint-absent failure regime and should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Neuro-symbolic methods that augment large language model (LLM) reasoning with formal solvers have demonstrated gains on logical reasoning benchmarks. Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} delegate formalization to external provers. More recent systems route problems to specialized solver paradigms \citep{xu2026dylos}, apply logic-complete decomposition \citep{li2025aristotle}, train dedicated first-order logic (FOL) verifiers on supervised data \citep{wang2025fover}, or employ multi-perspective grounding \citep{luo2025logicagent}. These systems report positive results on formal reasoning benchmarks, but a critical commonality unites them: each introduces capabilities beyond the reasoning model itself, whether trained verifiers, multi-paradigm solver selection, or external knowledge bases. The external machinery is effective but imposes practical costs in training data, integration complexity, and domain-specific engineering that limits portability.

These results raise a direct question: can the reasoning model itself extract useful formal constraints from its own traces? Same-model self-extraction would require no training data, no external prover, and no second model. Practitioners could augment any LLM with symbolic verification by adding a single extraction prompt and a satisfiability solver, with no domain-specific infrastructure. If successful, this approach would provide a lightweight, portable alternative to the external machinery that current systems require. Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extraction produces constraints useful for answer aggregation, or characterized the conditions under which it succeeds or fails. This gap is consequential: the practical promise of neuro-symbolic reasoning hinges on whether the reasoning model alone can supply formal structure of sufficient quality, or whether external grounding is fundamentally required.

Self-Consistency (SC) selects the most frequent answer across multiple chain-of-thought samples \citep{wang2023sc} and remains competitive across mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning \citep{chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc}. SC treats traces as black boxes, discarding all intermediate reasoning. Each trace, however, contains intermediate steps, logical dependencies, and structural relationships that could in principle ground aggregation in formal logic, adding discriminative power beyond vote counting. This would also address SC's known scaling plateau, where additional traces yield diminishing returns \citep{loo2025reevaluating}.

We evaluate this possibility through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), a pipeline that extracts FOL constraints from $K$ reasoning traces produced by a single LLM, deduplicates by syntactic equivalence, and solves a weighted partial MAX-SAT problem via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3}. The answer best supported by the largest satisfiable constraint subset is selected (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}). We test five model families spanning 7B to 32B parameters (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, QwQ-32B), including instruction-tuned models, a reasoning-specialized model, and a distilled reasoning model, across three reasoning domains: formal logic (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}), commonsense (StrategyQA \citep{geva2021strategyqa}), and science (ARC-Challenge \citep{clark2018arc}), with supplementary probes on GSM8K \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} and AIME 2024, totaling more than 1,300 instances. An oracle control on FOLIO ($n=204$) replaces self-extracted constraints with gold FOL annotations verified by Z3, isolating extraction quality from aggregation effectiveness following established methodology \citep{press2023compositionality}.

Across all conditions, SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over SC, with accuracy gaps between $-3.3$ and $+3.3$\,pp. The oracle experiment yields a fundamentally different result: $+8.82$\,pp over SC (McNemar $p = 6.15 \times 10^{-5}$), confirming that the MAX-SAT mechanism is sound when given discriminative constraints. The bottleneck is extraction quality. Because the same model generates both answers and constraints, the extracted constraints are semantically coupled to their source answers and carry no independent signal. We term this the \emph{capability trap}: the model cannot formalize corrections to its own reasoning errors because extraction inherits the same biases that produced those errors. A constraint ablation confirms the diagnosis: MAX-SAT and count-only aggregation agree on 803 of 804 predictions (\S\ref{sec:ablation}). Manual analysis shows only 11.5\% of unique constraints evaluate differently across candidates; the remainder encode shared domain facts that contribute identical scores to every answer. Constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total SICA pipeline time, roughly doubling wall-clock cost for zero expected accuracy gain.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item We evaluate SICA across five model families and three reasoning domains ($N > 1{,}300$), finding no improvement over majority voting in any condition.
\item We design an oracle control achieving $+8.82$\,pp over SC ($p < 0.001$), causally localizing the failure to extraction quality rather than the aggregation mechanism.
\item We identify the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ as a zero-cost diagnostic: low $C_0$ rules out any possible SICA gain before constraint extraction begins.
\item We show through constraint ablation that MAX-SAT, count-only, and random-weight aggregation produce nearly identical predictions (803/804 agreement), confirming that self-extracted constraints carry no discriminative signal beyond vote counts (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation across five model families (7B to 32B parameters) and three reasoning domains with more than 1,300 total instances. Self-extracted SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over Self-Consistency in any tested condition, with accuracy gaps ranging from $-3.3$ to $+3.3$\,pp. The oracle experiment, which replaces self-extraction with gold FOL annotations verified by Z3, achieves $+8.82$ percentage points over SC ($p < 0.001$). This result causally localizes the failure to extraction quality: the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound when supplied with high-quality constraints, but same-model self-extraction cannot produce them. We identify this as a \emph{capability trap}: because the reasoning model also extracts the constraints, those constraints inherit the same biases that produced potentially flawed answers and carry no independent discriminative signal. The failure is not one of aggregation design but of the circular dependency between generation and verification within a single model.

The practical consequences are substantial. Only 11.5\% of self-extracted constraints evaluate differently across candidate answers; the remainder encode shared domain facts satisfied equally by every candidate. MAX-SAT agrees with count-only aggregation on 803 of 804 predictions, which confirms that satisfiability structure adds nothing when constraints are non-discriminative. Constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total pipeline time and roughly doubles computational cost for zero expected accuracy benefit. For practitioners who evaluate constraint-based voting, the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ serves as a zero-cost diagnostic: it is computable from trace samples alone, before any investment in constraint extraction or solver invocation. Low $C_0$ rules out any possible SICA gain by construction, and high $C_0$ signals the need for a small-scale constraint quality audit before full deployment.

The $+8.82$\,pp oracle gap quantifies recoverable potential and points to three concrete paths forward. Trained FOL extractors supervised on gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns beyond same-model capabilities. Cross-model extraction, where a separate model formalizes another model's traces, breaks the self-reference loop that produces non-discriminative constraints. External provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency entirely. Each path targets the extraction bottleneck directly; the aggregation mechanism requires no modification.

\section{Prompt Templates}
\label{app:prompts}

SICA uses domain-specific prompt templates for constraint extraction: one for mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, AIME) and one for logical reasoning (ProofWriter, FOLIO). Both share the same system prompt. The LLM is called with temperature $T{=}0.1$, max tokens $1024$, and structured JSON output mode. Up to 6 traces are processed in parallel via thread pooling, with 2 retries on failure (exponential backoff, base 0.5s).

\paragraph{System Prompt.}

\begin{lstlisting}
You are a constraint extraction tool. Output ONLY
valid JSON. Do NOT solve problems, reason about
correctness, or think step-by-step. Extract
constraints from the given trace exactly as stated.
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Mathematical Constraint Extraction (EXTRACTION\_PROMPT).}

Used for GSM8K and AIME datasets. The placeholder \texttt{\{trace\}} is replaced with the reasoning trace at runtime.

\begin{lstlisting}
Extract mathematical constraints from this reasoning
trace as a JSON object.

Rules:
- type: "equation", "inequality", or "predicate"
- expression: human-readable, e.g. "x + y == 14"
- z3_formula: a single comparison expression in
  Python Z3 syntax
- source_step: step number where the constraint
  appears
- Use variable names from the trace

z3_formula MUST follow these rules:
- Allowed operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=, +, -, *,
  /, **, %
- Use individual named variables: a1, a2, a3...
  NOT arrays a[1] or sets A
- Expand all sums explicitly:
  "a1 + a2 + a3 == 55" NOT "sum([a1,a2,a3])"
- NO Python builtins: sum(), len(), max(), min(),
  list(), set(), range(), int()
- Each z3_formula must be exactly ONE comparison
  (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=)
- For multiple values, write separate constraints
  for each

Output ONLY the JSON below, nothing else:
{"constraints": [{"type": "equation",
  "expression": "x + y == 14",
  "z3_formula": "x + y == 14",
  "source_step": 1}],
 "answer": "final_answer",
 "variables": ["x", "y"]}

Trace:
{trace}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Logical Constraint Extraction (LOGIC\_EXTRACTION\_PROMPT).}

Used for ProofWriter and FOLIO datasets.

\begin{lstlisting}
IMPORTANT: You are an EXTRACTION tool, NOT a problem
solver.
- Do NOT re-solve or re-reason about the problem.
- Do NOT verify whether the trace's reasoning is
  correct.
- ONLY extract the logical constraints that are
  explicitly stated or used in the trace below.
- Output ONLY the JSON object, nothing else.

Extract logical constraints from this reasoning trace
about a logic problem.

The problem has facts (base assertions), rules
(grounded implications), and derived conclusions.
Convert each into a Z3 boolean formula.

Variable naming:
- Unary property: property_entity
  (e.g., kind_anne, red_charlie, round_fiona)
- Binary relation: relation_subject_object
  (e.g., eats_bear_squirrel, likes_lion_cat)
- Use lowercase with underscores only

Constraint types:
- "fact": a given assertion,
  e.g., kind_anne == True
- "rule": a grounded implication over specific
  entities, e.g., Implies(kind_anne, nice_anne)
- "derived": an inferred conclusion from facts +
  rules, e.g., nice_anne == True

Z3 operators:
- Implies(a, b) for if-then rules
- And(a, b, ...) for conjunctive conditions
- Or(a, b, ...) for disjunctive conditions
- Not(a) for negation
- == True / == False for boolean assertions

Output ONLY the JSON below, nothing else:
{"constraints": [{"type": "fact",
  "expression": "kind(anne)",
  "z3_formula": "kind_anne == True",
  "source_step": 1}],
 "answer": "True or False or Unknown",
 "variables": ["kind_anne"]}

Trace:
{trace}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Output Schema.}

Both prompts produce a JSON object with the following structure:

\begin{lstlisting}
{
  "constraints": [
    {
      "type": "<equation|inequality|predicate>
               or <fact|rule|derived>",
      "expression": "<human-readable description>",
      "z3_formula": "<Z3-compatible expression>",
      "source_step": <integer>
    }
  ],
  "answer": "<final answer string>",
  "variables": ["<var1>", "<var2>", "..."]
}
\end{lstlisting}

The pipeline additionally injects an \texttt{answer\_assertion} constraint per trace (not produced by the LLM):

\begin{lstlisting}
{"type": "answer_assertion",
 "expression": "answer is <ans>",
 "z3_formula": "__sica_answer_<ans> == True",
 "source_step": -1}
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Prompt Selection Logic.}

Domain assignment is determined by dataset: FOLIO and ProofWriter use \textsc{Logic\_Extraction\_Prompt}; MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME use \textsc{Extraction\_Prompt}.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation across five model families (7B to 32B parameters) and three reasoning domains with more than 1,300 total instances. Self-extracted SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over Self-Consistency in any tested condition, with accuracy gaps ranging from $-3.3$ to $+3.3$\,pp. The oracle experiment, which replaces self-extraction with gold FOL annotations verified by Z3, achieves $+8.82$ percentage points over SC ($p < 0.001$). This result causally localizes the failure to extraction quality: the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound when supplied with high-quality constraints, but same-model self-extraction cannot produce them. We identify this as a \emph{capability trap}: because the reasoning model also extracts the constraints, those constraints inherit the same biases that produced potentially flawed answers and carry no independent discriminative signal. The failure is not one of aggregation design but of the circular dependency between generation and verification within a single model.

The practical consequences are substantial. Only 11.5\% of self-extracted constraints evaluate differently across candidate answers; the remainder encode shared domain facts satisfied equally by every candidate. MAX-SAT agrees with count-only aggregation on 803 of 804 predictions, which confirms that satisfiability structure adds nothing when constraints are non-discriminative. Constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total pipeline time and roughly doubles computational cost for zero expected accuracy benefit. For practitioners who evaluate constraint-based voting, the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ serves as a zero-cost diagnostic: it is computable from trace samples alone, before any investment in constraint extraction or solver invocation. Low $C_0$ rules out any possible SICA gain by construction, and high $C_0$ signals the need for a small-scale constraint quality audit before full deployment.

The $+8.82$\,pp oracle gap quantifies recoverable potential; trained extractors, cross-model pipelines, and external provers each target the extraction bottleneck directly, as discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
